Say goodbye to Butterfingers, Crunch bars, Baby Ruths & more

Not much of a surprise to me, and really shouldn't be to anyone that has been alive long enough to watch K Mart, Target, and Wal-Mart grow to dominance.

Large retailers work on small profit margins and by doing so they strictly carry the best selling products. All shelf space is valuable resource, so if a product doesn't sell as fast as the other products, it gets changed out for another that might perform better. This has been very evident with the candy aisle. Most candy bars are impulse purchases at the checkout stand, and that is very, very valuable retail space. So what you wind up with is only a few candy bars being able to occupy that space. The selection shrinks, and like everything else in a big box retailer, your only option is the most popular items. If you want something different, you have to go to a specialty shop.

Simultaneously, the price of candy bars has gotten outrageous. They are no longer a cheap treat that you buy yourself, but they are now priced to the point where you actually balance the value vs the cost. Once a product like a candy bar gets to the point where the consumer thinks about the purchase for more than 1 second, you are losing customers.

Couple the two things together and it's a hard time being a candy that isn't one of the top 5 sellers.

What made America great was a simple five-word statement: "All men are created equal." At the time that was written, it was generally accepted throughout Western culture that rich people were inherently "better" than poor people. This was known as "deference," and the general population was expected to "defer to their betters" in essentially all matters. Additionally, social mobility was actively thwarted; aristocrats were shunned for marrying "beneath their station," and poor people could never "change their stars."

America flew in the face of that. Regardless of what the founders specifically meant by "men," they wanted all men to have the same opportunities for advancement, to "pursue happiness." It was a radical notion at the time and has enabled the "rags-to-riches" stories we hear even to this day.
